subject: technology
essential_question: How do we reason about attackers without ever touching a real system?
standards: Michigan Computer Science: Networks and the Internet — Cybersecurity
project_brief: Write a threat model and defensive hardening plan for a fictional system inside a sandbox; no live or third-party system is probed. This is the grade 10 culminating project for "Cybersecurity Foundations in a Sandbox" (ma-g10-technology-u05, unit 5), built around confidentiality integrity and availability, authentication and authorization concepts, encryption and hashing concepts, common vulnerability classes, and secure coding practices. Write a threat model and defensive hardening plan for a fictional system inside a sandbox; no live or third-party system is probed. Use only fictional examples, sandbox tools, or already-approved data — never a real account, real credential, or live external system.
requirements: Address every topic listed for this unit: confidentiality integrity and availability, authentication and authorization concepts, encryption and hashing concepts, common vulnerability classes, secure coding practices, and sandboxed defensive analysis.
Meet the performance task as written: Write a threat model and defensive hardening plan for a fictional system inside a sandbox; no live or third-party system is probed.
Show your work or process, not just a final result — a process note, sketch log, commit history, or draft trail.
Complete the checklist in this package before submitting.
primary_task: Write a threat model and defensive hardening plan for a fictional system inside a sandbox; no live or third-party system is probed. Use only fictional examples, sandbox tools, or already-approved data — never a real account, real credential, or live external system.
test_or_check_criteria: Every claim or design choice in the submission can be traced to confidentiality integrity and availability or another named topic from this unit — nothing is left unexplained.
The submission runs, displays, or demonstrates correctly on at least two different sample inputs or scenarios the student chooses.
No real password, API key, account credential, precise location, or other real personal/system data appears anywhere in the submission — fictional or sandbox examples only.
The student can explain, in their own words, why each step or decision was made, not just that it works.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: This project never touches a real account, a real password or API key, a live production system, or another person's real data. Use fictional names, sandbox environments, local files, or already-approved sample data throughout. Submit code, screenshots of your own sandbox, diagrams, or a written walkthrough — a live public deployment is never required.

copyright_and_authorship: The final submitted work must remain your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI assistant may help you plan, explain a concept, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but may not produce the graded work itself. Never request, store, or submit a real password, API key, access token, or other real credential; use only fictional accounts and sandboxed or offline systems.
remediation: If the project stalls, step back to the smallest version of the task: rebuild just the part covering confidentiality integrity and availability in isolation, using a worked example from this unit as a model, then re-attach it to the full project once that smaller piece works and you can explain why.
extension: Once the core project is working, extend it to handle a new constraint or edge case related to authentication and authorization concepts, or compare two different approaches to the same problem and explain the real tradeoff between them in your own words.
